facts.statehood_note: Iowa entered the Union as a free state. President James K. Polk signed the admission bill.
facts.motto: Our liberties we prize, and our rights we will maintain
facts.name_origin: Named after the Iowa River, which takes its name from the Ioway people.

government.chambers: Iowa Senate (50 senators, 4-year terms) and Iowa House of Representatives (100 representatives, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term). The governor leads the executive branch and appoints Supreme Court justices from a list of nominees chosen by the State Judicial Nominating Commission.
government.courts: Iowa Supreme Court (7 justices). The governor appoints justices from nominees sent by the State Judicial Nominating Commission; voters then decide in retention elections whether to keep them for regular 8-year terms. Justices must retire at age 72.
government.local: 99 counties with 100 county seats, because Lee County has two.
government.constitution: Iowa's current constitution dates from 1857. It changed Article I, Section 1 from "free and independent" to "free and equal," but at first still kept the vote from Black Iowans; voters added Black men's right to vote by amendment in 1868.
government.kid_line: "All men and women are, by nature, free and equal, and have certain inalienable rights" (Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: The Ioway lived on this land from the early 1600s and descend from the Oneota culture, who lived near the Mississippi River about 800 years ago. The state and the Iowa River are named for them; they were pushed out about a decade before statehood.

An Algonquian-speaking people from the Eastern Woodlands whom the French called "Renards" (the Fox), though they have always called themselves Meskwaki. They moved into Iowa in the mid-1700s after the French forced them out of the Great Lakes region.

Allies of the Meskwaki since 1735, the Sauk and Meskwaki together controlled land from central Illinois to western Iowa, southern Wisconsin, and northern Missouri. Their language is close to Meskwaki.

long_ago.nation: Omaha, Ponca, Ioway, and Otoe-Missouria ancestors at Blood Run
long_ago.about: Ancestors of these nations lived at Blood Run on the Big Sioux River from about 900 to 1720 CE, a large village and ceremonial site that was a major trading center from about 1500 to 1700, drawn by game, fertile soil, and pipestone.
The Dakota and Ho-Chunk also lived in Iowa; the Ho-Chunk were forced out by treaty in 1848 and the Dakota in 1858.

Hopewell people, who hunted, gathered, and gardened, built burial mounds at Toolesboro about 200 BCE to 300 CE. Later Woodland-period peoples built more than 200 mounds at Effigy Mounds, 31 of them shaped like bears and birds.

today.nation: Sac and Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa (Meskwaki Nation)
today.about: The only federally recognized tribe in Iowa; the Meskwaki bought their first 80 acres in Tama County on July 13, 1857, and today own more than 8,100 acres in Tama, Marshall, and Palo Alto Counties.

first_peoples.today_note: The Meskwaki Settlement near Tama is the only Native American settlement in Iowa. Most Sauk and Meskwaki were removed to a reservation in Kansas in the 1840s, and members of the Iowa Tribe (Ioway) live today in Kansas, Nebraska, and Oklahoma.
sites: Effigy Mounds National Monument (Allamakee and Clayton Counties): 206 mounds, 31 shaped like bears and birds; the National Park Service recognizes ties to 20 tribes
Toolesboro Mounds National Historic Landmark (near Wapello): Hopewell burial mounds from about 200 BCE to 300 CE
Blood Run National Historic Landmark (Big Sioux River, Iowa and South Dakota): village, mounds, and trading site used from about 900 to 1720 CE

history.event: As the last glacier melts, the first people arrive in Iowa, hunting mammoths, ground sloths, and bison. Native peoples lived here for nearly 13,000 years before Europeans and Americans came.
Hopewell people build burial mounds at Toolesboro along the Mississippi River.
Woodland-period peoples build mounds in northeast Iowa, including animal-shaped mounds of bears and birds now protected at Effigy Mounds National Monument.
Ancestors of the Omaha, Ponca, Ioway, and Otoe-Missouria live and trade at Blood Run on the Big Sioux River.
French explorers Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet record Indigenous villages on the Iowa side of the Mississippi River.
Through the Louisiana Purchase, the United States claims present-day Iowa, land that Indigenous nations still lived on and governed.
After the Black Hawk War, the U.S. forces the Sauk and Meskwaki to give up land in the Black Hawk Purchase. On June 1, 1833, the land opens to white settlers.
Congress creates the Iowa Territory. In 1839 the territorial Supreme Court frees a man named Ralph, declaring, "No man in this territory can be reduced to slavery."
The Sauk and Meskwaki are pressured to give up all their remaining Iowa land for little payment and agree to move to Kansas.
Iowa becomes the 29th state, a free state. Still, its laws deny Black Iowans the vote, jury and militia service, and public schools, and an 1851 law bans Black people from settling in Iowa.

Iowa towns such as Grinnell and Salem are stops on the Underground Railroad, helping freedom seekers escaping slavery in Missouri. John Brown trains his men at Springdale before his raid on Harpers Ferry.
Iowa adopts its current constitution. On July 13 the Meskwaki buy 80 acres in Tama County, becoming the first tribe in the U.S. to buy back land after removal.
In the Civil War, Iowa sends more than 75,000 volunteers to the Union army; about 13,000 Iowans die, mostly from disease. Annie Wittenmyer of Keokuk leads work to improve Union hospitals.

An amendment to the Iowa Constitution gives Black men the right to vote, two years before the 15th Amendment, and the Iowa Supreme Court rules in Clark v. Board that Susan Clark can attend her Muscatine public school.

trailblazers.name: Alexander Clark
trailblazers.text: A Muscatine barber and businessman, he rallied support for a Black regiment in the Civil War and led the statewide fight that won Black men the vote in Iowa in 1868. He sued so his daughter could attend public school, earned a law degree in Iowa City in 1884, and became U.S. Minister to Liberia in 1890.

trailblazers.name: Susan Clark
trailblazers.text: In 1867, at age 12, she was turned away from a Muscatine public school because she was Black. Her family sued, and in 1868 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled that separate was not equal and ordered her admitted, long before the U.S. Supreme Court's Brown v. Board of Education.

trailblazers.name: Emma Coger
trailblazers.text: She was removed from the dining cabin of a Mississippi River steamboat because of her race. She sued, and in 1873 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled she had the same rights as white passengers, using the state constitution's promise that all people are free and equal.

trailblazers.name: Arabella Mansfield
trailblazers.text: A graduate of Iowa Wesleyan College in Mount Pleasant, she passed Iowa's bar exam in 1869 even though state law limited it to men, becoming the first woman licensed as a lawyer in the United States. She chaired the Iowa Women's Suffrage Convention in 1870.

trailblazers.name: Amelia Bloomer
trailblazers.text: She edited The Lily, the first newspaper by and for women, before settling in Council Bluffs in 1855. She was the first Iowan to speak publicly for women's right to vote, founded a Soldier's Aid Society in the Civil War, and led the Iowa Suffrage Association from 1871 to 1873.

trailblazers.name: George Washington Carver
trailblazers.text: Born in Diamond Grove, Missouri, he studied at Simpson College in Indianola and became the first Black student at Iowa State Agricultural College in Ames, graduating in 1894. He became its first Black graduate student and faculty member, then taught at Tuskegee Institute for 47 years.

trailblazers.name: Frank Sanache (Meskwaki Code Talkers)
trailblazers.group: Meskwaki man, World War II Code Talker
trailblazers.text: Frank Sanache was one of eight Meskwaki men from Tama County, along with Willard Sanache, Dewey Youngbear, Edward Benson, Judie Wayne Wabaunasee, Mike Wayne Wabaunasee, Dewey Roberts, and Melvin Twin, who served as scouts and Code Talkers in North Africa during World War II. He was captured by German forces and held prisoner. When he died in August 2004 he was the last of the Meskwaki Code Talkers, and the Iowa Senate passed a resolution honoring the group.

landforms: Loess Hills (wind-blown silt hills along the western border)
Driftless Area (steep hills and valleys in the northeast)
Hawkeye Point, the highest point (1,670 feet)
Rolling plains and prairie potholes left by glaciers
waters: Missouri River and Big Sioux River (western border)
Spirit Lake and West and East Okoboji Lakes
Saylorville Lake, Lake Red Rock, Coralville Lake, and Rathbun Lake (human-made)
geography.regions: Glaciers shaped most of Iowa into rolling plains once covered by tallgrass prairie, with the Loess Hills rising along the Missouri River in the west and the steep hills and valleys of the Driftless Area in the northeast.

ecosystems.name: Tallgrass prairie
ecosystems.about: About 85 percent of Iowa was once prairie, with grasses taller than 6 feet, but less than one-tenth of one percent of its 30 million acres remains. Prairie remnants hold big bluestem, purple coneflower, and butterflies like the regal fritillary.

ecosystems.name: Loess Hills prairie
ecosystems.about: These dry hills shelter rare prairie life such as the prairie rattlesnake, the Great Plains toad, and the bobolink, and The Nature Conservancy grazes a herd of bison there.

ecosystems.name: Prairie potholes and fens
ecosystems.about: Glaciers that melted about 10,000 years ago left thousands of shallow wetlands called prairie potholes; fens are wet, alkaline places full of sedges and reeds.

ecosystems.name: Oak savanna and river woodlands
ecosystems.about: Savanna is grassland with scattered oak trees, and woods grew along Iowa's rivers and streams; the 2020 derecho flattened about a quarter of Iowa's forest.

science.weather: Iowa has a humid continental climate with hot summers and cold winters. It averages about 47 tornadoes a year and about 50 days of thunderstorms. On August 10, 2020, a derecho (a long line of straight-line windstorms) hit with gusts up to 126 mph, flattening about 850,000 acres of crops and half of Cedar Rapids' tree canopy. Floods and drought also strike; the 2020–2023 drought hit Iowa especially hard.
science.resources: Rich prairie soil makes Iowa the nation's top producer of corn and ethanol, along with soybeans and hogs; food processing leads its manufacturing. Northwest Iowa has some of the largest concentrations of wind turbines in the world.
science.highlight: The Loess Hills: Ice Age glaciers ground rock into fine silt, and winds blew it off the Missouri River floodplain into drifts more than 200 feet deep. Loess this deep is matched only in China.

g3_ss.title: Iowa's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Des Moines, the 99 counties, and the rivers on Iowa's borders, and learn what the General Assembly, governor, and Supreme Court do.

g3_ss.title: Iowa's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Ioway, Meskwaki, and Sauk, visit the bear and bird mounds at Effigy Mounds, and learn how the Meskwaki bought back their land in 1857.

g3_ss.title: Iowa Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Alexander and Susan Clark, Arabella Mansfield, Amelia Bloomer, George Washington Carver, and Frank Sanache and the Meskwaki Code Talkers.

g45_ss.title: Iowa's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study Hopewell and Woodland mound builders, the Blood Run trading center, and the Ioway, Meskwaki, Sauk, Dakota, and Ho-Chunk homelands.

g45_ss.title: Treaties and the Iowa Territory
g45_ss.plan: Trace Marquette and Jolliet, the Louisiana Purchase, the Black Hawk War and land cessions, the Iowa Territory, and the Case of Ralph.

g45_ss.title: Iowa 1846–1877: Free State, War, and Equal Rights
g45_ss.plan: Examine statehood as a free state with unequal laws, the Underground Railroad, the Meskwaki land purchase, the Civil War, and the 1868 victories for Black voting and school rights.

g3_sci.title: The Prairie Sea
g3_sci.plan: Learn how tall prairie grasses, flowers, and butterflies live together and why so little prairie is left.

g3_sci.title: Storm Safety in Iowa
g3_sci.plan: Learn about thunderstorms, tornadoes, and the 2020 derecho, and how families stay safe.

g3_sci.title: Rocks and Geodes
g3_sci.plan: Crack open the state rock and learn how crystals grow inside geodes.

g45_sci.title: Hills Built by Wind
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how glaciers and wind made the Loess Hills and compare them to deposits in China.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers and Wetlands
g45_sci.plan: Study how melting glaciers left prairie potholes and fens and why wetlands matter for wildlife.

g45_sci.title: From Prairie Soil to Farm Fields
g45_sci.plan: Explore Iowa's soil, corn, and wind energy, and what prairie restoration and bison grazing do for the land.
